title: The Salt March to Dandi and Dharasana
intro: Mohandas Gandhi, leader of the Indian National Congress's campaign of nonviolent civil disobedience, set out on foot from the Sabarmati Ashram with 78 satyagrahis to break the British salt monopoly at the coastal village of Dandi. The march of about 24 days passed through 4 districts and 48 villages.
ending: Gandhi broke the salt law at Dandi on 6 April 1930 and was arrested on the night of 4 to 5 May. At Dharasana, police clubbed the unresisting satyagrahis, and more than sixty thousand Indians were jailed as a result of the Salt Satyagraha.

stops.text: Gandhi and 78 satyagrahis set out on foot from the ashram for Dandi, 385 km away. On the eve of the march thousands came to hear him at the evening prayer.
stops.quote: On 12 March 1930, Gandhi and 78 satyagrahis, among whom were men belonging to almost every region, caste, creed, and religion of India, set out on foot for the coastal village of Dandi in Navsari district of Gujarat, 385 km from their starting point at Sabarmati Ashram.

stops.text: The marchers reached Nadiad from Matar on the fourth day. In each village crowds greeted them with drums and cymbals, and Gandhi attacked the salt tax as inhuman.
The marchers arrived from Nadiad on 16 March and rested here for a day. Each night they slept in the open and asked the villagers only for food and water to wash with.
stops.quote: Day 6. Rest Day in Anand: 17 March 1930

stops.text: The march crossed the Narmada River on the way from Derol to Ankleshwar. Every day more people joined, until the procession was at least 3 km long.
stops.quote: Day 15. Derol to Ankleshwar (Crossing the Narmada River): 26 March 1930

stops.text: After crossing the Tapi River from Delad the marchers entered Surat, where 30,000 people greeted them. Foreign journalists and three Bombay cinema companies were filming newsreels along the route.
stops.quote: Day 21. Delad to Surat (Crossing the Tapi River): 1 April 1930

stops.text: The marchers went on from Vanz to Navsari on 3 April, two days before they arrived at the seashore at Dandi.

Gandhi reached the seashore on 5 April. Next morning he raised a lump of salty mud, declaring that he was shaking the foundations of the British Empire, and boiled it in seawater to make illegal salt. He urged his followers to do the same.
stops.quote: When Gandhi broke the British Raj salt laws at 8:30 am on 6 April 1930, it sparked large-scale acts of civil disobedience against the salt laws by millions of Indians.

stops.text: After Gandhi broke the salt laws, about 700 telegrams were sent from the post office nearest to Dandi, most of them by the journalists who had come to report the news.
stops.quote: After the Gandhi broke the salt laws, about 700 telegrams were sent out from the post office nearest to Dandi, at Jalalpur.

stops.text: Gandhi set up a temporary ashram near Dandi. Around midnight of 4 May, while he slept on a cot in a mango grove, the District magistrate of Surat arrived with two Indian officers and thirty heavily armed constables and arrested him.
stops.quote: Around midnight of 4 May, as Gandhi was sleeping on a cot in a mango grove, the District magistrate of Surat drove up with two Indian officers and thirty heavily armed constables.

stops.text: Gandhi was arrested under an 1827 regulation calling for the jailing of people engaged in unlawful activities. He was held without trial near Poona, now Pune.
stops.quote: He was arrested under an 1827 regulation calling for the jailing of people engaged in unlawful activities, and held without trial near Poona (now Pune).

stops.text: Abbas Tyabji and Kasturba Gandhi were arrested before reaching Dharasana, and Sarojini Naidu led the march on. Soldiers clubbed the satyagrahis with steel tipped lathis, and they did not resist. Webb Miller reported fractured skulls and broken shoulders, and police kicking the seated men and dragging them into ditches.
stops.quote: Soldiers began clubbing the satyagrahis with steel tipped lathis in an incident that attracted international attention.

notes: Dates of the march stops come from the article's March Route list (arrival day of the line; Anand's 17 March is its rest day; the article says 5 and 6 April at Dandi). Left out: other villages of the list (Navagam, Matar, Borsad, Ankhi, Amod, Samni, Derol, Mangrol, Umracchi, Bhatgam, Delad, Vanz, Matwad), which the article names with no event; Peshawar (Qissa Khwani) and Vedaranyam, which Gandhi did not visit. Dharasana and Jalalpur: the article gives no date, so date and year are null. The article says Dandi was 'called Navsari at that time'; the Navsari stop uses the route list. Dandi twice because the journey returned to the coast; the 4 May place (mango grove) is only 'near Dandi' by the article's account of the temporary ashram. The Dharasana beating is not dated in the article. Wp titles for Kareli, Aslali, Jalalpur are guesses at Wikipedia titles; check.
